title: System Prompts, Roles & Structured Contracts
description: The system/user/assistant role structure, how to write an effective system prompt, treating structured output as a strict contract, and managing conversation state across turns.

lessons.title: System, User, and Assistant: The Three Roles
lessons.description: Understand the message-role structure every LLM API call is built on.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what the system, user, and assistant roles each contribute to a conversation.

sections.title: 🎭 Three roles, one conversation
sections.content:
Every call to a chat-style LLM API is built from a list of role-tagged messages: **system** (instructions and policy, set once, usually invisible to the end user), **user** (what the actual person typed), and **assistant** (the model's own previous replies, included so it can see the conversation history it's continuing).

```python
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a concise, friendly support assistant."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "How do I reset my password?"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Go to Settings > Security > Reset Password."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What if I don't have access to my email?"},
]
```

sections.title: 🔁 Why history has to be resent every time
sections.content: The model itself has no memory between API calls — each call is stateless. The full conversation history is resent as part of the messages list every single time, which connects directly to the token-budget concerns from the transformers and generative AI courses: a long conversation gets more expensive and eventually risks hitting context limits, covered later in this module.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Putting end-user-facing instructions in the system role expecting the user to see them.** The system message is typically invisible to the person chatting; it's policy for the model, not a message to display.

**Forgetting to include prior assistant turns in a multi-turn conversation.** Without them, the model has no memory of what it already said and can contradict itself.

**Treating the roles as decorative labels rather than something the model was specifically trained to treat differently.** Models are trained to weigh system instructions differently from user requests — the distinction has real behavioral effect, not just organizational convenience.

questions.question: What is the typical purpose of the 'system' role in a chat-style LLM API call?
options: It contains what the end user actually typed
It sets instructions and policy for the model, usually invisible to the end user, established once at the start of the conversation
It only contains the model's previous replies
It has no functional difference from the user role
questions.explanation: The system role is where policy and behavioral instructions live — tone, constraints, persona — typically set once and not shown to the end user, distinct from what the user actually says.

questions.question: Why must the full conversation history be resent with every API call to a chat model?
options: It doesn't need to be resent; the model remembers previous calls automatically
The model itself is stateless between calls, so the full message history has to be included each time for the model to have access to the conversation so far
Resending history is optional and has no effect on the model's responses
Only the very first message ever needs to be sent
questions.explanation: Since the model has no built-in memory across separate API calls, the entire relevant conversation history — system, prior user turns, and prior assistant turns — must be included in each new request for continuity.

questions.question: Why does it matter that models are specifically trained to treat the system role differently from the user role?
options: It doesn't matter — all roles are treated identically as plain text
Because of that training, the system role instructions genuinely carry different behavioral weight than user messages, rather than being just an organizational label with no functional effect
Only the user role has any effect on the model's behavior
The assistant role is the only one that affects the model's future output
questions.explanation: The role structure isn't just for human readability — models are trained to weigh system-role content as policy-level instruction distinct from user requests, giving the role distinction genuine behavioral consequence.

questions.question: In the example message list from this lesson, which role contains what the actual end user typed?
options: The user role
The system role
The assistant role
There is no role for the end user's input
questions.explanation: The lesson's example shows the user role holding the actual text the person typed, distinct from the system role's policy and the assistant role's prior replies.

questions.question: Why does the lesson include the assistant's own previous replies in the messages list?
options: So the model can see the conversation history it's continuing, since it has no memory between calls
Because the assistant role is required by the API even if empty
So the user can edit the assistant's past replies before sending
Because assistant messages are converted into system messages automatically
questions.explanation: Previous assistant replies are included precisely because the model itself has no memory between calls — without them, it would have no way to know what it already said in the conversation.

questions.question: Why is putting end-user-facing instructions in the system role a common mistake, according to this lesson?
options: Because the system message is typically invisible to the person chatting; it's policy for the model, not something meant to be displayed
Because the system role is always shown directly to the user by every API
Because system messages are limited to exactly one sentence
Because only the assistant role can contain instructions
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that the system role is generally not shown to the end user, so instructions meant for the person to actually see and read don't belong there.

questions.question: What happens if prior assistant turns are forgotten when building a multi-turn conversation, per this lesson?
options: The model has no memory of what it already said and can contradict itself
The model automatically recalls its past replies from a separate memory store
Nothing changes; the conversation continues exactly the same way
The user role silently takes over the assistant's missing content
questions.explanation: The lesson lists this as a common mistake: without prior assistant turns included, the model has no way to know what it already told the user, risking contradictions.

questions.question: According to this lesson, why do the system, user, and assistant roles have more than just organizational significance?
options: Because models are trained to weigh system instructions differently from user requests, giving the role distinction real behavioral effect
Because the roles are purely cosmetic labels with no effect on model behavior
Because only the user role has any influence on the model's output
Because roles only matter when tool calling is involved
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly states that treating the roles as merely decorative is a mistake — models are trained to treat system-role content differently, so the distinction carries genuine behavioral weight.

lessons.title: Structured Output as a Contract, Not a Suggestion
lessons.description: Apply the constrained decoding concept from an application-engineering perspective.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain why treating an LLM's output format as a strict contract changes how you build around it.

sections.title: 🤝 Downstream code needs a guarantee, not a best effort
sections.content: The generative AI course covered constrained decoding as a technique; here, the engineering question is: your downstream code (a database write, a UI render, another function call) needs the LLM's output to reliably match an expected shape. A best-effort text response that's usually well-formatted JSON isn't good enough for code that will crash or silently misbehave on the exceptions.

sections.title: 🧾 Schema-first design
sections.content:
Define the exact schema you need first (field names, types, required vs. optional), then use structured-output features (JSON mode, function-calling-style schemas, or constrained decoding) to enforce it, and validate the result programmatically before using it downstream — never trust unvalidated model output the same way you wouldn't trust unvalidated user input.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class TicketSummary(BaseModel):
    category: str
    priority: int  # 1-5
    one_line_summary: str

# Parse and validate the model's output against this schema
# before it's ever used by downstream code
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Skipping validation because the model 'usually' gets it right.** 'Usually' isn't a guarantee — validate every time, especially for anything feeding an automated pipeline.

**Treating a schema violation as a crash instead of a handled case.** Plan a fallback path (retry, default value, human escalation) for when validation fails, rather than letting it take down the whole pipeline.

**Over-engineering the schema for a simple use case.** Match schema complexity to what downstream code actually needs — a schema with 20 fields for a task that uses 3 of them adds unnecessary failure surface.

questions.question: Why is a 'best-effort' text response that's usually well-formatted JSON not sufficient for production downstream code?
options: Best-effort responses are always perfectly reliable in practice
Downstream code that expects a specific structure will crash or silently misbehave on the exceptions where the output doesn't match, so a strict guarantee matters more than a good average case
JSON formatting has no relevance to downstream code at all
Downstream code never actually depends on the exact shape of LLM output
questions.explanation: Code that expects a specific data shape needs reliability on every call, not just most of the time — the exceptions where formatting slips are exactly what cause crashes or silent bugs in an automated pipeline.

questions.question: What does 'schema-first design' mean in the context of LLM structured output?
options: Writing the prompt first and hoping a reasonable structure emerges naturally
Defining the exact expected schema (field names, types, required/optional) up front, then using structured-output features to enforce it and validating the result against that schema
Never using any schema at all, to maximize flexibility
Schema-first design only applies to database systems, not LLM applications
questions.explanation: Schema-first design means deciding what shape you need before generating anything, then enforcing and validating against that definition — rather than generating first and hoping the result happens to be usable.

questions.question: Why is it important to have a fallback path for when output validation fails, rather than letting it crash the pipeline?
options: Validation never actually fails in practice, so a fallback is unnecessary
A validation failure is an expected, handleable case (like a retry, default value, or escalation), and treating it as a full pipeline crash creates unnecessary fragility
Fallback paths make a system less reliable, not more
Crashing the pipeline is always the correct response to any validation failure
questions.explanation: Since output can occasionally fail to match a schema even with structured-output techniques, planning a graceful fallback (retry, default, escalation) keeps the system resilient instead of letting a single formatting slip take down the whole pipeline.

questions.question: In this lesson's example, what tool is used to define and validate the expected schema for the model's output?
options: A Pydantic BaseModel
A raw regular expression
A manually written string parser with no schema
An unstructured free-text template
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example uses a Pydantic BaseModel (TicketSummary) to define the exact expected fields and types, which the model's output is then validated against.

questions.question: According to this lesson, how should you treat unvalidated model output compared to unvalidated user input?
options: The same way — never trust unvalidated model output any more than you'd trust unvalidated user input
Model output should always be trusted completely without validation
User input needs validation but model output never does
Validation is only needed for tool-call arguments, not general structured output
questions.explanation: The lesson draws a direct parallel: unvalidated model output deserves the same skepticism and validation discipline as unvalidated user input before it's used downstream.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against skipping validation because the model 'usually' produces correct output?
options: Because 'usually' isn't a guarantee, and validation matters especially for anything feeding an automated pipeline
Because the model always produces perfectly valid output with no exceptions
Because validation is only relevant for text generation, not structured output
Because skipping validation always improves pipeline reliability
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly states that 'usually' correct isn't sufficient for a pipeline — validating every time protects against the exceptions where the model's output doesn't match the expected shape.

questions.question: Why does the lesson advise against over-engineering a schema for a simple use case?
options: Because schema complexity should match what downstream code actually needs — an overly complex schema for a simple task adds unnecessary failure surface
Because simple schemas are always technically invalid
Because more fields in a schema always improve reliability
Because Pydantic cannot support schemas with more than a few fields
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is building an overly complex schema (e.g. 20 fields) for a task that only needs a handful, which needlessly adds more ways for validation to fail.

questions.question: What kind of fallback options does this lesson recommend when structured-output validation fails?
options: A retry, a default value, or human escalation, rather than letting the failure crash the whole pipeline
There is no recommended fallback; validation failures should always be ignored
The only acceptable fallback is stopping the application entirely
Fallbacks are unnecessary since validation never actually fails
questions.explanation: The lesson recommends planning a handled fallback path — retry, default value, or escalation — for validation failures, rather than treating a schema violation as an unhandled crash.

lessons.title: Managing Conversation State Across Turns
lessons.description: Handle multi-turn conversations correctly as they grow over time.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can describe how conversation state is maintained across turns and what has to be managed as it grows.

sections.title: 📚 State lives in your application, not the model
sections.content: Since the model itself is stateless (from the first lesson), your *application* is responsible for storing and managing conversation state — typically the running list of messages — and deciding what to include on each new call. This is a genuine engineering responsibility, not something the LLM API handles for you automatically.

sections.title: ✂️ Growing conversations need active management
sections.content:
As a conversation grows, simply appending every new message forever eventually hits context window and cost limits (from the transformers and generative AI courses). Real applications need a strategy: truncating old turns, summarizing earlier parts of the conversation into a condensed form, or retrieving only the most relevant prior context rather than all of it.

```python
# Conceptual: a simple truncation strategy
def build_context(system_prompt, history, max_turns=10):
    return [system_prompt] + history[-max_turns:]
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Appending every message forever with no limit.** This works fine in a demo and then breaks (or gets expensive) in real, longer-running usage.

**Summarizing too aggressively and losing important early context.** A summary that drops a detail the user references later ('like I mentioned earlier...') creates a confusing user experience.

**Storing conversation state insecurely or without considering data retention policy.** Conversation history often contains sensitive user information and needs the same data-handling care as any other user data.

questions.question: Why is managing conversation state a responsibility of the application rather than something the LLM handles automatically?
options: The LLM automatically remembers all past conversations across every call
The model itself is stateless between calls, so the application must store and decide what conversation history to include in each new request
Conversation state management is not actually necessary for any LLM application
Only the very first message in a conversation needs to be tracked
questions.explanation: Since each API call to the model is independent and stateless, it's entirely up to the calling application to maintain, store, and decide what history to resend — a genuine engineering task, not an automatic model feature.

questions.question: Why can't a real application simply append every new message to the conversation forever with no limit?
options: There is no actual limit; conversations can grow indefinitely with no consequence
A conversation that grows without bound eventually hits context window limits and increasing per-call cost, both covered in earlier courses
Appending messages has no relationship to cost or context limits
Applications are only ever used for single-turn conversations
questions.explanation: Every additional message adds tokens to what must be resent on each call, and unbounded growth eventually collides with context window limits and rising cost — exactly the token-budget concerns raised in the transformers and generative AI courses.

questions.question: What is a risk of summarizing earlier parts of a long conversation too aggressively?
options: Summarization has no downsides and should always be maximized
An overly aggressive summary can drop details the user later references, creating a confusing experience when the assistant seems to have 'forgotten' something specific
Summarization always improves conversation quality with no tradeoff
Summaries are never used in real conversation management strategies
questions.explanation: If a summary compresses away specific details, a user who later refers back to something specific ('like I mentioned earlier') can find the assistant appears to have lost that context — a real UX cost of over-aggressive summarization.

questions.question: In the conceptual truncation strategy shown in this lesson, what does the build_context function keep from the conversation history?
options: Only the most recent max_turns messages, combined with the system prompt
The entire unbounded history regardless of length
Only the very first message ever sent
A random sample of messages from the whole conversation
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example shows a simple truncation strategy that keeps the system prompt plus only the last max_turns entries of history, rather than the full unbounded conversation.

questions.question: Besides truncation, what other strategies does this lesson mention for managing a growing conversation?
options: Summarizing earlier parts of the conversation, or retrieving only the most relevant prior context
Deleting the system prompt after the first turn
Always sending the complete, unaltered history regardless of length
Switching to a completely different API for every new turn
questions.explanation: The lesson lists summarizing earlier parts of a conversation into condensed form, or retrieving only the most relevant prior context, as additional strategies alongside truncation.

questions.question: Why does the lesson flag storing conversation state insecurely as a common mistake?
options: Because conversation history often contains sensitive user information and needs the same data-handling care as any other user data
Because conversation state is never sensitive and requires no special handling
Because only system prompts need secure storage, never user messages
Because storing conversation history is always illegal regardless of method
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly warns that conversation history can contain sensitive information, so it needs the same careful handling and consideration of data retention policy as any other user data.

questions.question: Why does this lesson describe appending every message forever as working fine in a demo but breaking in real usage?
options: Because it eventually hits context window and cost limits once conversations grow long enough in real, longer-running usage
Because demos and production environments have identical scaling behavior
Because appending messages has no relationship to context window limits
Because only production systems have a context window, not demos
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that unlimited appending works in a short demo conversation but eventually collides with real context window and cost limits once usage grows longer in production.

questions.question: Why is application-level state management described as a 'genuine engineering responsibility' in this lesson?
options: Because the model itself is stateless, so the application must handle storing and deciding what history to include on each call
Because the LLM API automatically manages all conversation state without any application involvement
Because state management is entirely optional and has no effect on functionality
Because only the model provider is responsible for conversation state, never the developer
questions.explanation: Since the model has no built-in memory across calls, the lesson emphasizes that it's squarely the calling application's job to store and manage what conversation state gets included in each new request.
